definition: Catalyze means to set a process in motion or speed it up.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word catalyze. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know catalyze should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The new rail stop catalyzed a wave of construction, and within three years the empty lots around it had become a neighborhood.
A nudge is gentler than catalyzing — it inches something forward once, while catalyzing sets a whole process running faster than it could run on its own.
Unleash is stronger than catalyze — a catalyzed process still runs in an orderly way, but an unleashed one bursts out past anyone's control.

To spark something is to supply the first flash that starts it, and the word's work ends there. To catalyze goes further: whatever catalyzes a change both starts it and speeds it, staying behind the process like an engine rather than a single match.

To trigger something is to set it off when it was already primed and waiting, like a tripwire — the release happens at once. To catalyze a change is different: the change is a running process, and the catalyst makes it run faster than it would alone.

To kindle something is to start it small and feed it slowly, the way a first flame is coaxed along with twigs. To catalyze is brisker — a catalyzed process visibly accelerates, gaining speed it could never have found on its own.

The library's seed exchange began with one shoebox of envelopes, but it catalyzed something larger: a garden club, then a farmers' stall, then a course at the community center, each started by people who first met over that box.
Catalyze is borrowed from chemistry, where a catalyst speeds a reaction without being used up.
That is the nuance to keep: whatever catalyzes a change is a spark and an accelerator, not the raw material of the change itself.
Catalyze is the writer's word for a spark with an engine behind it — a grant, an event, or a person that gets change moving faster.
Prefer trigger for something primed to go off anyway, and spark for the bare first flash; catalyze earns its place when the process visibly accelerates.

When the library added a small recording booth, the town's teen podcast scene did not exactly begin there — two shows already existed, limping along on phone microphones.
But the booth catalyzed everything.
Within a month the two shows doubled their output; within six, nine new programs had launched, sharing editing tips on a corkboard by the door.
The librarians did not host, script, or edit a single episode.
They only kept the booth running — an engine humming under a process that was already in motion.
A visiting reporter put it simply: the booth turned a slow hobby into a fast-moving scene, and it never once appeared on the air.
